title: The Late Pleistocene Megafauna Extinction
intro: Between roughly 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most land mammal species weighing over 44 kg went extinct across Australia, Eurasia, and the Americas. Two scientists discuss the cause.

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: Overkill hypothesis
figures.text: The extinctions were caused primarily by human hunting. The timing of the losses tracks the arrival of modern humans on each landmass rather than any global climate event: Australia lost its megafauna around 45,000 years ago, shortly after human arrival, while North America lost its megafauna about 13,000 years ago, again shortly after human arrival. Africa, where hominins and megafauna coevolved over millions of years, retained most of its large mammals — precisely what one would expect if naive prey animals were the vulnerable ones. Large, slow-reproducing species need only a small sustained increase in mortality to decline toward extinction; models show that a kill rate of a few animals per hunter per year is sufficient over centuries.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Climate hypothesis
figures.text: The extinctions were caused primarily by rapid climate change at the end of the last glacial period. Between 15,000 and 11,000 years ago, warming fragmented the cold, dry, productive "mammoth steppe" into forest and wetland, collapsing the habitat that supported grazing megafauna. Pollen records show vegetation turnover preceding or coinciding with the losses on multiple continents. Direct kill sites are rare: fewer than 20 North American sites show unambiguous evidence of humans butchering mammoths or mastodons, far too few to account for continent-wide extinction. Moreover, several species survived for millennia alongside humans before disappearing, which is inconsistent with rapid hunting-driven collapse.

title: What Caused the Younger Dryas Cooling?
intro: About 12,900 years ago, the Northern Hemisphere abruptly cooled by several degrees for roughly 1,200 years, reversing a warming trend. Two scientists discuss the cause.

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: Meltwater hypothesis
figures.text: A vast glacial lake in North America drained suddenly into the North Atlantic. The influx of fresh water reduced surface salinity and density, weakening the ocean circulation that carries warm water northward. Weakening that circulation cools northern Europe and eastern North America while leaving the Southern Hemisphere little changed — exactly the asymmetric pattern the ice-core and pollen records show. Sediment cores from the St. Lawrence outlet record a discharge event at approximately the right time.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Impact hypothesis
figures.text: A comet or asteroid fragmented over the ice sheet, triggering continent-scale wildfires whose soot blocked sunlight and initiated cooling. A thin sediment layer dated to 12,900 years ago contains elevated platinum, magnetic microspherules, and nanodiamonds at dozens of sites across three continents — materials associated with extraterrestrial impacts and not produced by lake drainage. The abruptness of the onset, within decades, favors a sudden catastrophic trigger over a gradual oceanographic change.

title: Effect of Catalyst Concentration on Reaction Rate
text:
A student investigated how the concentration of a catalyst affects the speed of a color-change reaction between two solutions. In each trial, the student combined the two solutions with a fixed volume of catalyst solution at a given concentration. The student then used a stopwatch to record the time, in seconds, until the mixture turned from clear to blue. All trials were run at a constant temperature of 25 degrees C. Reaction rate is defined as 1 divided by the time required for the color change, measured in inverse seconds (s^-1). A larger rate means a faster reaction.

The student first tested Catalyst X at five concentrations (see Table 1). The student then repeated the experiment at the same five concentrations using Catalyst Y, a different compound. The completion times for both catalysts were plotted together (see Figure 1).

title: Three Explanations for Desert Varnish
text:
Desert varnish is a thin, dark coating of iron and manganese oxides that forms on exposed rock surfaces in arid regions. It can take centuries to accumulate a layer less than a millimeter thick, and the coating darkens further the longer it remains exposed. Three geologists studying the same varnished rock outcrop proposed different explanations for where the coating's minerals originally come from.

Geologist 1
Geologist 1 argues that the varnish forms from within the rock itself. Many desert rocks contain small amounts of iron and manganese bound up in their internal mineral structure. Geologist 1 proposes that rainwater rarely but occasionally seeps into surface cracks and pores, where it slowly dissolves these trace minerals. The water then evaporates quickly, which is typical of an arid climate. As it evaporates, it deposits the dissolved iron and manganese as a thin film on the rock's outer surface. Repeated over thousands of cycles of wetting and evaporation, this film thickens into visible varnish. Under this view, the varnish's composition should closely mirror the mineral makeup of the rock beneath it. The coating, in this account, is made from material that migrated outward from the rock's own interior rather than arriving from anywhere else.

Geologist 2
Geologist 2 rejects a purely chemical explanation and points instead to microorganisms living directly on the rock surface. Certain bacteria are known to gain usable energy by chemically oxidizing manganese, a process that leaves behind solid manganese oxide as a byproduct. Geologist 2 proposes that these bacteria colonize the rock surface in a thin biological film. As they grow, the bacteria absorb trace manganese and iron carried by windblown dust and moisture, and deposit the oxidized metals directly onto the rock. Because the responsible organisms are living things rather than a passive chemical process, this hypothesis makes a distinct prediction. A rock's varnish should be able to form even on rock types that contain little or no iron or manganese of their own, since the metals arrive from outside sources rather than leaching from within the rock.

Geologist 3
Geologist 3 attributes the varnish almost entirely to windblown dust. Deserts generate large quantities of fine airborne particles, some of which carry trace iron and manganese picked up from distant soils. Geologist 3 proposes that this dust settles continuously on exposed rock surfaces. Thin films of moisture from dew or occasional rain bind the particles to the rock and to each other, gradually cementing them into a hardened crust. Because the source of the minerals is external dust rather than the rock's own composition or living organisms, this hypothesis makes a distinct prediction of its own. Varnish from different rock outcrops in the same region should share a similar chemical makeup regardless of what kind of rock lies underneath, since all of the outcrops in an area receive dust from the same regional source.

title: Fading of a Dye Under Light
text:
A dye dissolved in water absorbs blue light, and the amount it absorbs is reported as absorbance. Absorbance falls as the dye breaks down. Students prepared identical dye solutions and measured absorbance with a meter. All samples were held at 22 degrees C in a water bath.

Study 1

title: Why Is the Blue-Spotted Tree Frog Declining in Cedar Hollow?
text:
Over the past 15 years, the population of blue-spotted tree frogs in Cedar Hollow, a forested wetland, has declined by more than 70 percent. Researchers agree on the extent of the decline but disagree about its primary cause. Three biologists studying the wetland have proposed different explanations.

Biologist 1
Biologist 1 attributes the decline primarily to a fungal skin infection that has been detected on frogs throughout the region. The fungus disrupts a frog's ability to regulate water and electrolytes through its skin, which can be fatal within weeks of infection. Biologist 1 notes that the fungus thrives in cool, wet conditions similar to those in Cedar Hollow, and that infected frogs have been found at every site sampled in the wetland. Under this view, the decline should track the spread of the fungus itself rather than any change in the physical habitat. Populations in wetlands where the fungus has not yet arrived should remain stable, even if those wetlands closely resemble Cedar Hollow in every other respect.

Biologist 2
Biologist 2 points instead to agricultural runoff. Farms upstream of Cedar Hollow began using a new pesticide roughly 18 years ago. Biologist 2 argues that trace amounts carried into the wetland by rainwater have interfered with the frogs' hormone systems, reducing successful reproduction even among adults that otherwise appear healthy. Biologist 2 notes that the timing of the decline follows the introduction of the pesticide more closely than it follows any known arrival of disease. Under this view, reproductive success should be lowest closest to the streams that drain the farmland. Wetlands with no agricultural runoff nearby should show a much smaller decline, even if the fungus described by Biologist 1 is also present there.

Biologist 3
Biologist 3 argues that the decline is best explained by an invasive fish species, introduced to Cedar Hollow's ponds around 20 years ago for recreational fishing, that preys heavily on frog eggs and tadpoles. Biologist 3 notes that ponds within the wetland that remain fish-free still support relatively dense frog populations, while ponds stocked with the invasive fish show far fewer frogs at every life stage. Under this view, the decline should correlate closely with the presence of the invasive fish from pond to pond within Cedar Hollow itself, regardless of disease exposure or nearby farmland. Removing the fish from a pond should allow the frog population there to recover over time.

title: Growth of Radish Seedlings Under Different Watering Schedules
text:
Radish seeds were planted in identical pots of the same potting soil and kept under identical grow lights. Seedling height was measured in centimeters from the soil surface to the tallest leaf tip. Relative growth rate is defined in this study as the change in height divided by the number of days elapsed.

Study 1
Five groups of seedlings (10 per group) were watered on different schedules: once every 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 days, with 20 mL of water per watering. Height was measured after 21 days (see Table 1).

Study 2
Two additional groups were watered once every 1 day or once every 4 days. Height was measured every 7 days for 28 days (see Figure 1).

Iron corrodes (rusts) when it combines with other substances to form a solid product. In each trial below, a cleaned iron nail of initial mass 5.00 g was sealed in a test tube and held at 22 °C for 14 days. The nail and any solid product were then dried and weighed together; an increase in mass indicates that corrosion occurred, and a larger increase indicates more corrosion.

Study 2

Nails were given various coatings and then sealed in moist air, matching the fourth condition of Study 1. The painted nail was deliberately scratched through to the metal before sealing.

Study 3

Nails were immersed in sodium chloride (NaCl) solutions of varying concentration, each open to an air space.

title: Frost Cracking in Sandstone
intro:
Water expands as it freezes. When water fills the pore spaces inside a rock and then freezes, the expansion pushes outward on the pore walls. Geologists studied whether repeated freezing could break sandstone, and if so, what controls how quickly it happens.

Porosity is the percentage of a rock's volume made up of pore space.

Experiment 1

Cylindrical cores were cut from four sandstones of differing porosity. Each core was soaked in water for 48 hours, then placed in a chamber that cycled once per hour between +5 °C and −10 °C. Cores were inspected after every cycle, and the cycle at which a crack first became visible was recorded.

Experiment 2

The procedure of Experiment 1 was repeated using only 12% porosity cores, but the minimum temperature of the cycle was varied. The maximum remained +5 °C.

Experiment 3

The procedure of Experiment 2 was repeated with 12% porosity cores that had been oven-dried for 72 hours and kept sealed from moisture. Each core was cycled 300 times.

title: The Trout of Lake Idris
intro:
Lake Idris supported a lake trout population for as long as records exist. Lake trout need cold water and also need dissolved oxygen; in summer the lake separates into a warm surface layer and a cold deep layer, and the fish are confined to whatever water satisfies both requirements. Between 1995 and 2020 the catch fell by more than 90%, and by 2020 no trout were found. Two limnologists proposed different explanations.

Scientist 1

The lake warmed. Mean August surface temperature rose 2.6 °C over the period, and the boundary between the warm and cold layers sank steadily deeper. Each summer the band of water cold enough for trout grew thinner, until in the hottest years it closed entirely for several weeks. Trout that cannot escape warm water stop feeding, grow slowly, and fail to spawn. The decline tracks air temperature almost year for year, and the three steepest single-year drops in catch all followed the three hottest summers on record. Oxygen in the deep layer did fall, but that fall is itself a consequence of warming: a warmer, longer-stratified summer keeps the deep layer sealed off from the air for more weeks each year.

Scientist 2

The lake lost its oxygen. Farm acreage in the watershed doubled after 1990, and the phosphorus entering the lake rose with it. Phosphorus feeds algae; when the algae die they sink and decay, and decay consumes oxygen in exactly the deep, cold water the trout depend on. Measured August oxygen in the deep layer fell from 8.1 mg/L to 1.9 mg/L, well below the 4 mg/L that lake trout require. The cold water never disappeared — it simply became unbreathable. Warming may have made matters worse at the margins, but a 2.6 °C rise in surface temperature does not by itself remove a deep layer that is still 6 °C in August.
